Anderssen gives away both rooks, a bishop and finally his queen, and still checkmates with his three remaining minor pieces. The most famous attacking game of its time.
A quiet position suddenly explodes: Anderssen sacrifices his queen and finishes with a beautiful mate by two bishops. It is called evergreen because its beauty never fades.
Played in a box at the Paris Opera during a performance. Morphy brings out his pieces quickly and ends with a queen sacrifice and mate: a perfect lesson in development.
The first world champion leaves his rook to be taken and gives check after check with the other. Rather than be mated, von Bardeleben quietly left the hall, and Steinitz showed the public the mate.
One of the shortest famous games: a queen sacrifice on move 9, then a double check, and mate by a bishop on move 11.
Thirteen-year-old Bobby Fischer gives up his queen on move 17 and wins with a storm of minor pieces. A chess writer called it the game of the century.
Kasparov gives up a rook and chases Topalov’s king across the whole board. It is often called one of the most beautiful games ever played.
